title: The Time Capsule
summary: A class buries a time capsule filled with letters and small objects, to be dug up and opened again ten years later.
poll: It is worth the effort to write a letter to your future self.

versions.title: The Time Capsule
versions.text:
Our class made a box today. We call it a time capsule. We will bury it. We will dig it up in ten years.

Our teacher is Mr. Faisal. He told us to write a letter. "Tell me your hopes for the future," he said. Lina wrote hers first. She hopes to be a doctor. She also hopes for more books.

Then we talked. What might change? Omar said cars might fly. Huda said robots might help at home. We all liked to guess.

We put our letters in the box. We put small things in, too. A toy. A card. A coin.

The box is made of tin. Rain can not get in.

We will put it under the big tree. We will put a rock on top. The date is on the rock.

In ten years, we will dig it up. We will open the box. We will read what we wrote.

versions.title: The Time Capsule
versions.text:
Imagine burying a box today. You would not open it again until you finish university. That is almost ten years. Ten years is also called a decade.

That is exactly what our class decided to do this year. We made a time capsule. A time capsule is a sealed box. It holds letters, photographs, and small objects. We plan to open it again long after it is buried.

Our teacher, Mr. Faisal, explained why we do this. He said a time capsule helps preserve memories. It is like sending a message to our older selves, a message for the next generation. Then he told us to write a letter. It should tell our hopes for the future.

Lina was the first student to finish her letter. She wrote that she hopes to become a doctor one day. She wants to help sick people in her town. She also hopes our school will get new computers and a bigger library. No one could truly predict what the future might bring. That made the project both exciting and a little mysterious.

After writing, our class talked about the future. Omar guessed that cars might fly above the rooftops. Huda guessed that robots might help families clean their homes. Everyone enjoyed imagining how different daily life might become.

Next, we placed our letters inside the capsule. We added a toy, a photograph, and an old coin. The capsule is made of strong, sealed metal. It keeps water from getting inside and damaging our letters.

Afterward, our class buried the capsule under the tall tree. We placed a flat stone on top to mark the spot. We carefully wrote the date on the stone so no one would forget.

Ten years from now, our class plans to return to this spot. We will dig up the capsule together. We will finally read our old letters out loud. We will compare our guesses with how the future actually turned out.

versions.title: The Time Capsule
versions.text:
Ten years can feel like an entire lifetime when you are only in Grade 5. That is exactly why our class decided to build a time capsule this year, a small archive meant to carry our present selves into the future.

A time capsule is a sealed container that holds letters, photographs, and small personal objects, intended to be reopened long after it was first buried. People have constructed time capsules for well over a century, often sealing them inside the cornerstones of new buildings. Workers occasionally unearth these forgotten containers decades later, discovering newspapers, coins, and letters written by people who had long since grown old or passed away.

Our teacher, Mr. Faisal, explained that writing to the future is really a kind of legacy, a message meant for posterity rather than for anyone sitting in the room that day. He told us to write a letter describing our hopes for the future, and to bring one small object from home that matters to us. Lina finished her letter first, writing that she hopes to become a doctor so that she can help sick people in her town. She also anticipates that our school will eventually have new computers and a much larger library.

Afterward, the class speculated together about how daily life might change. Omar guessed that cars might fly above the rooftops within a decade. Huda imagined robots helping families clean their homes and prepare meals. Everyone enjoyed picturing a future that still felt exciting and slightly uncertain.

Next, we carefully placed our letters and small objects, including a toy, a photograph, and an old coin, inside the sealed metal capsule, which keeps water from damaging anything stored within it. We then buried the capsule under the tall tree beside our school garden. We marked the exact spot with a flat stone, carefully engraving the date so that no future visitor would overlook it.

In ten years, our class intends to return to this very spot. We will dig up the capsule together and finally compare our old predictions with whatever the future actually brought.

versions.title: The Time Capsule
versions.text:
Ten years can feel like an entire lifetime when you are only in Grade 5, which is precisely why our class decided to undertake a time capsule project this year, an unassuming archive intended to carry our present selves forward into a future we could only imagine, however imperfectly.

A time capsule is a sealed container that holds letters, photographs, and small personal objects, intended to be reopened long after it was originally buried, frequently by the very people who had once sealed it shut. People have constructed time capsules for well over a century, frequently embedding them inside the cornerstones of new buildings. Workers occasionally unearth these forgotten containers decades afterward, discovering newspapers, coins, and letters written by individuals who had long since grown old or passed away entirely, their handwriting the only trace that remained.

Our teacher, Mr. Faisal, explained that writing to the future is essentially a kind of legacy, a message intended for posterity rather than for anyone presently occupying the classroom, and that the entire endeavor requires a genuine curiosity about lives not yet lived. He instructed us to write a letter describing our hopes for the future, and to bring one small object from home that matters to us. Lina finished her letter first among all twenty-seven students, writing that she hopes to become a doctor so that she might help sick people throughout her town, and that she anticipates our school will eventually acquire new computers and a considerably larger library than the one we currently use.

Afterward, the class speculated together about how daily life might transform within a single decade. Omar guessed that cars might fly above the rooftops, while Huda imagined robots helping families clean their homes and prepare meals automatically, without any adult supervision whatsoever. Everyone enjoyed picturing a future that felt simultaneously exciting and somewhat uncertain, since nobody could say with any confidence which guesses would eventually prove correct.

Next, we carefully placed our letters and small objects, including a toy, a photograph, and an old coin, inside the sealed metal capsule, a container specifically engineered to prevent water from damaging anything stored within it over such an extended period. We subsequently buried the capsule beneath the tall tree beside our school garden. We marked the exact spot with a flat stone, carefully engraving the date so that no future visitor would ever overlook it.

In ten years, our entire class intends to return to this very spot and dig up the capsule together. We will finally compare our old predictions with whatever the future actually brought, however accurate or mistaken those particular guesses eventually turn out to be, recognizing that even a simple classroom exercise can function as a genuine archive of childhood, however small and ordinary that childhood might have seemed to us at the time.

versions.title: The Time Capsule
versions.text:
Our class decided to undertake a time capsule project this year, constructing an unassuming archive intended to carry our present selves forward into a future none of us could fully imagine. A time capsule, for those unfamiliar with the concept, is simply a sealed container holding letters, photographs, and small personal objects, meant to be reopened long after it was originally buried, frequently by the very people who had sealed it shut years earlier. People have constructed such capsules for well over a century, often embedding them inside the cornerstones of new buildings, and workers occasionally unearth these forgotten containers decades afterward, discovering newspapers, coins, and letters written by individuals who had long since grown old or passed away, their handwriting the only trace that remained of an otherwise ordinary life.

Our teacher, Mr. Faisal, framed the entire exercise as a kind of legacy, explaining that a letter written today becomes a message intended for posterity rather than for anyone presently occupying the classroom, and that constructing such a message requires genuine curiosity about lives not yet lived. Lina, finishing her letter before any of the other twenty-seven students, wrote that she hopes to become a doctor so that she might help sick people throughout her town, anticipating that our school would eventually acquire new computers and a considerably larger library than the modest one we currently use. Meanwhile, the rest of the class speculated enthusiastically about how daily life might transform within a single decade: Omar guessed that cars might eventually fly above the rooftops, while Huda imagined robots helping families clean their homes and prepare meals entirely without adult supervision, and everyone seemed to enjoy picturing a future that felt both exciting and genuinely uncertain.

Once our letters were finished, we carefully placed them alongside small personal objects, including a toy, a photograph, and an old coin, inside a sealed metal capsule engineered specifically to prevent water from damaging anything stored within it over such an extended period. We subsequently buried the capsule beneath the tall tree beside our school garden, marking the exact spot with a flat stone upon which we carefully engraved the date, ensuring that no future visitor would ever overlook its significance.

In ten years, our entire class intends to return to this very spot, dig up the capsule together, and finally compare our old predictions against whatever the future actually brought, however accurate or mistaken those particular guesses eventually turn out to be. Even a simple classroom exercise, we have come to realize, can function as a genuine archive of childhood, however small and ordinary that childhood might have seemed to us at the time, and perhaps that is precisely why such projects endure across generations of students who will likely never meet one another.

versions.title: The Time Capsule
versions.text:
Our class decided to undertake an ambitious time capsule project this year, constructing what amounted to an unassuming archive intended to carry our present selves forward into a future none of us could fully anticipate. A time capsule, for those unfamiliar with the concept, constitutes simply a sealed container holding letters, photographs, and small personal objects, meant to be reopened long after it was originally interred, frequently by the very individuals who had sealed it shut years, or even decades, earlier. People have constructed such capsules for well over a century, often embedding them inside the cornerstones of new buildings, and construction workers occasionally unearth these long-forgotten containers decades afterward, discovering newspapers, coins, and letters written by individuals who had long since grown old or passed away, their handwriting the only tangible trace that remained of an otherwise ordinary existence.

Our teacher, Mr. Faisal, framed the entire exercise as a kind of legacy, explaining that a letter composed today becomes, in effect, a message intended for posterity rather than for anyone presently occupying the classroom, and that constructing such a message requires genuine curiosity about lives not yet lived and circumstances not yet known. Lina, finishing her letter before any of the other twenty-seven students, wrote that she hopes to become a doctor so that she might help sick people throughout her town, anticipating that our school would eventually acquire new computers and a considerably larger library than the comparatively modest one we currently use. Meanwhile, the remainder of the class speculated enthusiastically about how daily life might transform within a single decade: Omar guessed that cars might eventually fly above the rooftops, while Huda imagined robots helping families clean their homes and prepare meals entirely without adult supervision, and nearly everyone seemed to relish picturing a future that felt simultaneously exciting and genuinely uncertain.

Once our letters were finished, we carefully placed them alongside small personal objects, including a toy, a photograph, and an old coin, inside a sealed metal capsule engineered specifically to prevent water from infiltrating and damaging anything stored within it over such an extended period. We subsequently buried the capsule beneath the tall tree beside our school garden, marking the exact spot with a flat stone upon which we meticulously engraved the date, thereby ensuring that no future visitor would ever overlook its considerable significance.

In ten years, our entire class intends to return to this very spot, excavate the capsule together, and finally compare our earlier predictions against whatever the future actually brought, however accurate or mistaken those particular guesses eventually turn out to be. Even an ostensibly simple classroom exercise, we have come to realize, can function as a genuine archive of childhood, however small and unremarkable that childhood might have seemed to us at the time, and perhaps that is precisely why such projects endure across successive generations of students who, in all likelihood, will never meet one another face to face.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Two friends who build many kites until one finally flies
A class that makes a time capsule to open in ten years
A class that visits a doctor
A class that builds robots for a contest
questions.why: The story is about a class that makes and buries a time capsule to be opened again in ten years.

wrong.A: This is a different story about kites, not time capsules.
wrong.C: Lina hopes to become a doctor, but that is only one small detail.
wrong.D: Robots are only something the class guesses about, not the main topic.

an astronaut
a robot maker
a doctor

help the whole school save a lot of money
questions.why: Mr. Faisal explains that a time capsule helps preserve memories for the next generation, like a message across time.

wrong.A: The article does not connect the capsule with library books.
wrong.C: The article does not say the capsule teaches robot-building.
wrong.D: The article does not mention saving money.

questions.stem: Where do people often seal time capsules, according to the article?
options: inside school libraries far away
underneath rivers and deep lakes
inside the cornerstones of new buildings
inside old wooden classroom desks
questions.why: The article says people have often sealed time capsules inside the cornerstones of new buildings.

wrong.A: The article does not mention school libraries for this detail.
wrong.B: The article does not mention rivers or lakes.
wrong.D: The article does not mention classroom desks.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they happen in the story.
options: The class buries the capsule; students write letters; Mr. Faisal explains the project
Students write letters; the class buries the capsule; Mr. Faisal explains the project
The class buries the capsule; Mr. Faisal explains the project; students write letters
Mr. Faisal explains the project; students write letters; the class buries the capsule
questions.why: Mr. Faisal first explains the project, then the students write their letters, and only afterward does the class bury the capsule.

wrong.A: The class cannot bury the capsule before writing the letters that go inside it.
wrong.B: Mr. Faisal explains the project before any letters are written.
wrong.C: The capsule cannot be buried before the letters are written.

questions.stem: In the article, the word preserve means —
options: to keep something safe so it lasts
to throw something far away forever
to make a sound much louder
to copy something else exactly
questions.why: The article uses preserve to mean keeping memories safe so they last for the next generation.

wrong.B: Preserving something is the opposite of throwing it away.
wrong.C: Preserve has nothing to do with sound.
wrong.D: Preserving is not the same as copying.

questions.stem: Why does the article say no one can truly predict the future?
options: because computers can already tell us the future
because the future has not happened yet, so it is uncertain
because Mr. Faisal already knows what will happen
because the capsule contains a prediction machine
questions.why: Since the future has not happened yet, it is impossible to know for certain what will occur, making it both exciting and mysterious.

wrong.A: The article does not mention computers predicting the future.
wrong.C: Mr. Faisal does not claim to know the future.
wrong.D: The capsule holds letters and objects, not a machine.

questions.stem: What can you infer about Lina from her hope to become a doctor?
options: She dislikes helping other people very much
She does not enjoy going to school at all
She cares about helping sick people in her community
She wants to work with robots instead someday
questions.why: Lina's wish to become a doctor so she can help sick people shows that she cares about helping others in her community.

wrong.A: Wanting to become a doctor shows the opposite: she likes helping people.
wrong.B: The article gives no sign she dislikes school.
wrong.D: Robots are something Huda guesses about, not Lina's goal.

questions.stem: How are Omar's and Huda's predictions about the future similar?
options: Both predict that school will be cancelled forever
Both predict that it will rain every single day
Both predict that robots will fully replace all teachers
Both predict that technology will help people in new ways
questions.why: Omar predicts flying cars and Huda predicts helpful robots; both guesses involve technology making life easier in new ways.

wrong.A: Neither prediction is about cancelling school.
wrong.C: Huda's guess is about helping with chores, not replacing teachers.

MID.prompt: Explain why the class decided to make a time capsule and how they prepared it. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained why the class made the time capsule.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.

keyWords.definition: to expect something or prepare for it before it happens
keyWords.example: The scientists anticipated that the experiment would take several months.

keyWords.definition: something passed down or left behind for people in the future
keyWords.example: The old library building is part of the town's historical legacy.

keyWords.definition: people who will be born in the future, especially later generations
keyWords.example: The artist painted the mural so that it would survive for posterity.

keyWords.definition: a collection of historical documents or records kept safely over time
keyWords.example: The museum keeps old newspapers in a locked archive.

keyWords.definition: to form a guess about something without being completely sure
keyWords.example: Scientists speculate about what life might be like on other planets.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the article?
options: A simple classroom project becomes a genuine legacy for the future.
Time capsules are much too fragile to survive underground for very long.
Only famous, historic buildings are ever allowed to contain time capsules.
Robots will eventually and completely replace the need for time capsules.
questions.why: The article shows how an ordinary classroom project becomes a meaningful legacy connecting the students' present to their future.

wrong.B: The article describes capsules designed to survive underground safely.
wrong.C: The article mentions ordinary buildings, not only famous ones.
wrong.D: Robots are only something the class imagines, not a replacement for capsules.

questions.stem: Why does the article say that workers sometimes discover old time capsules filled with newspapers and coins?
options: Because capsules are specially built to attract curious explorers
Because people have sealed capsules in buildings for a century and they later get uncovered
Because newspapers are required by old laws to be buried underground
Because coins placed underground naturally multiply in number over time
questions.why: The article explains that people have sealed time capsules in buildings for over a century, which is why workers later find them during construction.

wrong.A: The article does not say capsules are built to attract explorers.
wrong.C: The article does not mention any law about burying newspapers.

questions.stem: According to the article, what does Lina anticipate for her school by the time the capsule is opened?
options: that the school will close completely and forever
that the school will move to a brand new country
that the school will have new computers and a larger library
that the school will completely stop teaching science
questions.why: Lina anticipates that her school will eventually have new computers and a considerably larger library.

wrong.A: The article never says the school will close.
wrong.B: The article never mentions the school moving.
wrong.D: The article does not mention dropping science.

questions.stem: In the article, the word posterity refers to —
options: a kind of sealed metal container
a teacher who explains class projects
a tool used to dig under a tree
people who will live in future generations
questions.why: The article uses posterity to mean the future generations who will eventually read the letters.

wrong.A: A container is the capsule itself, not posterity.
wrong.B: Posterity does not mean a teacher.
wrong.C: Posterity is not a digging tool.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about Mr. Faisal's goal in framing the letters as a 'legacy'?
options: He wants students to see their words as meaningful beyond the present moment
He wants students to forget about the project quickly
He believes the letters will be read the very next day
He thinks posterity means the same thing as the present
questions.why: By calling the letters a legacy, Mr. Faisal encourages students to see their writing as meaningful far beyond the day it was written.

wrong.B: Framing it as a legacy is meant to make the project memorable, not forgettable.
wrong.C: The letters will be read ten years later, not the next day.
wrong.D: Posterity refers to the future, which is the opposite of the present.

questions.stem: Which best describes the order of events in the article?
options: The capsule is dug up fully; letters are then written; the class speculates about the future
Mr. Faisal explains the project; letters are written; the class speculates; the capsule is buried
The class speculates about the whole future; the capsule is buried; letters are written
The capsule is buried first; Mr. Faisal explains the project; letters are written afterward
questions.why: Mr. Faisal first explains the project, then letters are written, then the class speculates about the future, and finally the capsule is buried.

wrong.A: The capsule cannot be dug up before it is even buried.
wrong.C: Letters must be written before the capsule can be buried.
wrong.D: Mr. Faisal explains the project before the capsule is buried, not after.

questions.stem: How does the article compare the class's time capsule project to time capsules sealed in building cornerstones?
options: It argues that classroom capsules are more scientifically accurate than real ones
It claims that only grown adults are ever allowed to bury real time capsules
It shows that both serve a similar purpose: preserving messages for the future
It explains that cornerstone capsules are always found again within just one year
questions.why: Both the classroom capsule and the cornerstone capsules are described as ways of preserving messages and objects for people long in the future.

wrong.A: The article never compares scientific accuracy between the two.
wrong.B: The article does not say only adults may bury time capsules.
wrong.D: The article says cornerstone capsules are found decades later, not within a year.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article by calling the project 'a genuine archive of childhood'?
options: To argue that archives should contain only official government documents
To suggest that all of children's school projects have no lasting value
To explain in detail exactly how big museums collect objects
To emphasize that an ordinary school activity can hold real meaning
questions.why: Calling the project an archive of childhood emphasizes that even a simple classroom activity can carry lasting meaning.

wrong.A: The article does not argue archives must be official documents.
wrong.B: The phrase suggests the opposite: the project does have lasting value.
wrong.C: The article is not explaining museum collection methods.

HIGH.prompt: The poll asks whether it is worth the effort to write a letter to your future self. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the article about legacy, history, and prediction.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
